Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
\int \frac{3\,\text{d}x}{|9x|\sqrt{(9x)^{2}-1}}=3\int \frac{\text{d}x}{|9x|\sqrt{(9x)^{2}-1}}.
$$

This integral now resembles the basic one for $\text{arcsec},$

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\text{d}u=\text{arcsec}(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $9x.$

So, let's substitute $u=9x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=9\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{9}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}3\int \frac{1}{|9x|\sqrt{(9x)^{2}-1}}\text{d}x & =3\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\cdot (\frac{1}{9}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{\text{d}u}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\text{arcsec }u+C \\  & =\frac{\text{arcsec}(9x)}{3}+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

\int \frac{2\,\text{d}x}{|x|\sqrt{4{x}^{2}-1}}=4\int \frac{\text{d}x}{|2x|\sqrt{(2x)^{2}-1}}.
$$

This integral now resembles the basic one for $\text{arcsec},$

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\text{d}u=\text{arcsec}(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $2x.$

So, let's substitute $u=2x.$ Differentiating, we get

\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.

Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{9}{81+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{9}{81\cdot (1+{x}^{2}/81)}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}/81}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1+(x/9)^{2}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C.
$$

 The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{9})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{9}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{9}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=9\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{9}{81+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1+(x/9)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\cdot (9\,\text{d}u) \\  & =\int \frac{\text{d}u}{1+{u}^{2}} \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{9})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we can write this integral as

$$
{\int }_{0}^{1/2}\frac{2}{5+20{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{2}{5}{\int }_{0}^{1/2}\frac{1}{1+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent,

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $4{x}^{2}=(2x)^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=2x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.
$$

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $0$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $1$ |

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1/2}\frac{2}{5+20{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{2}{5}{\int }_{0}^{1/2}\frac{1}{1+(2x)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{5}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\cdot (\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{\text{d}u}{1+{u}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{arctan}⁡u{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(1)-\operatorname{arctan}⁡(0)) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\cdot \frac{\pi }{4} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{20}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-0.2}^{0.2}\frac{3}{\sqrt{3-75{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =3{\int }_{-0.2}^{0.2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3\cdot (1-25{x}^{2})}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{\sqrt{3}}{\int }_{-0.2}^{0.2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-25{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{-0.2}^{0.2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(5x)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

  

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(5x)}^{2}.$   

So, let's substitute $u=5x.$ Differentiating, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=5\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{5}\text{d}u.
$$

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $-0.2$ | $0.2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $-1$ | $1$ |

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-0.2}^{0.2}\frac{3}{\sqrt{3-75{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{-0.2}^{0.2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(5x)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{-1}^{1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot (\frac{1}{5}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{5}{\int }_{-1}^{1}\frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{5}\,\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u{|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{5}(\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(1)-\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(-1)) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{5}(\frac{\pi }{2}+\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}\,\pi }{5}\end{aligned}
$$
